## Major Hepatectomy and Extended Hepatectomy


- **Definition:** Resection of three or more contiguous hepatic segments
- **Scope:** Technical aspects of major and extended hepatic resections
- **Exclusions:** Biliary/vascular resections, living donor hepatectomy, minimally invasive focus

## Introduction to Major Hepatectomy

- Encompasses right and left hemihepatectomies
- Includes extended left and right hepatectomies
- Extended hemihepatectomies may include:
  - Small subsegmental portions of adjacent parenchyma
  - Formal "trisectionectomy" (adjacent segments IV or V/VIII)
- Caudate lobe may be included in any of these resections

## Definition and Operative Risk

- Term "major hepatectomy" reflects technical challenge and significant morbidity
- Highest rates of postoperative morbidity among liver resections
- Key life-threatening complications:
  - Postoperative hepatic failure
  - Hemorrhage
  - Biliary complications
- Same principles apply regardless of open or minimally invasive approach

## Indications Overview

- **Most common:** Malignant tumors of the liver and biliary tree
- **Rare:** Large symptomatic or premalignant benign tumors
- **En bloc resections:** Perihepatic tumors involving diaphragm, adrenal, retroperitoneum, stomach, duodenum
- **Benign conditions:** Infections, trauma, complex bile duct injuries
- Diagnostic hepatic resection for indeterminate mass is rarely indicated today

## Parenchymal-Sparing Philosophy

- Major hepatectomy should be an operation of **last resort**
- Parenchymal-sparing operations preferred whenever possible
- Rationale: less hepatic parenchyma removed = less postoperative morbidity
- Removal of three or fewer segments rarely results in liver failure
- Major hepatectomy only when pathology involves inflow/outflow vessels mandating hemiliver removal

## Volume Considerations and FLR

- **Right hemiliver:** approximately two-thirds of total liver volume
- **Right liver + segment IV:** can occupy over 80% of liver volume
- **Left hemiliver resections:** relatively low-volume even when extended
- **Right posterior sector:** variable volume
- **Left trisectionectomies:** majority leave future liver remnant (FLR) >30%
- FLR volume directly responsible for posthepatectomy morbidity

## Preoperative Planning: Imaging Requirements

- **Mandatory:** High-quality multiphasic cross-sectional imaging
  - Arterial and portal venous phases
- Assess:
  - Extent of disease
  - Vascular proximity
  - Anatomic variation
- Evaluate branching patterns of hepatic veins, portal veins, and hepatic artery
- Both MRI and CT provide necessary detail; each has specific advantages

## Preoperative Planning: Biliary Assessment

- Biliary anomalies relatively common
- Preoperative recognition of branching abnormalities is important
- **Most common anomalies:**
  - Right sectoral ducts draining to left bile duct
  - Low insertions into common hepatic/bile duct
- **Imaging of choice:** MRCP with gadolinium contrast
- MRCP with Eovist contrast and specific CT protocols also useful
- Most relevant for **left-sided** major resections

## Preoperative Planning: Liver Function Assessment

- **Child-Pugh scoring:** simple, easily obtainable, clinically useful
- **Critical addition:** Assess for portal hypertension (not in Child-Pugh)
- Portal hypertension can result from:
  - Chronic liver disease
  - Extensive systemic chemotherapy
- Clinical findings: splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, varices
- Large-volume resections only in Child-Pugh A with no portal hypertension

## Preoperative Planning: FLR Assessment

- Direct measurement of FLR volumes should be liberally assessed
- **FLR <25–30%:** significant risk of posthepatectomy liver failure
- Higher volume thresholds in:
  - Chronic liver disease
  - Chemotherapy-related hepatic injury
- **Portal vein embolization:** consider when volumes inadequate
- Assessment of volume growth kinetics improves safety of major resections

## Anatomy: Hepatic Artery

- Common hepatic artery branches off celiac axis
- Courses to right along superior border of pancreatic body
- Gives off gastroduodenal artery, then right gastric artery
- Proper hepatic artery branches into right and left hepatic artery
- Left hepatic artery runs cephalad along left border of porta hepatis toward umbilical fissure

## Hepatic Artery: Distal Branching

- Distal left hepatic artery most commonly branches at base of umbilical fissure into:
  - Segment IV branch
  - Left lateral section branch (segments II and III)
- Segment IV branch can arise from proximal right hepatic artery
- Right hepatic artery courses cephalad, to the right, typically posterior to common hepatic bile duct (90%)
- If anterior to duct (10%), it is the most anterior structure in right porta hepatis

## Hepatic Artery Anomalies

- **Replaced vessels:** originate from branch other than hepatic artery; completely replace supply
- **Accessory vessels:** supply portion of hemiliver in conjunction with standard inflow
- **Replaced/accessory right hepatic arteries:** from superior mesenteric artery; course posteriorly along right porta hepatis lateral to portal vein
- **Replaced/accessory left hepatic arteries:** from left gastric artery; run through gastrohepatic ligament to base of umbilical fissure
- Common hepatic artery can be replaced to superior mesenteric artery

## Anatomy: Portal Vein

- Forms from confluence of splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein
- Courses toward liver posteriorly and to the right within porta hepatis
- At base of liver between caudate lobe and segment IV:
  - Splits into long transverse leftward running **left portal vein**
  - Shorter, more cephalad coursing **right portal vein**
- First branches to caudate lobe must be identified before encircling right or left portal vein

## Portal Vein: Caudate and Left Branches

- Caudate branch off right portal vein arises proximally and supplies caudate process
- Left portal vein gives off significant caudate branch before curving into umbilical fissure
  - Supplies left side of caudate
  - Adjacent to insertion of ligamentum venosum
- Small segment IV portal vein branches branch superiorly off transverse portion of left portal vein
- Left portal vein typically branches into left liver segments intrahepatically

## Portal Vein Anomalies

- Posterior sectoral branches often originate without common posterior sectoral portal vein
- **5–10% of patients:** early branching posterior sectoral vein directly off main portal vein
- **Very rare (1%):** single branch enters liver substance; gives off right portal vein, then courses left yielding left portal vein
  - Dangerous: easy to mistakenly divide whole portal venous anatomy
- Preservation of portal venous inflow critically important for postoperative regeneration

## Anatomy: Bile Duct

- Common bile duct located anteriorly along right border of porta hepatis
- Common hepatic duct defined cephalad to variable insertion of cystic duct
- Biliary tree supplied by hepatic artery branches at 3 and 9 o'clock positions
- Skeletonization of lateral aspects can result in ischemia, strictures, or necrosis
- **Left bile duct:** long, courses transversely along base of segment IV, enters umbilical fissure
- **Right bile duct:** short, early branching into sectoral/segmental branches at base of cystic plate

## Bile Duct Anomalies

- Both right and left bile ducts provide drainage to caudate lobe
- Left-sided caudate branches drain into left bile duct
- Caudate process/right side branches drain into right bile duct
- **Most relevant anomaly:** right sectoral branches into left bile duct
  - Right posterior or anterior sectoral duct entering left bile duct
  - Particularly relevant for left-sided major resections
- Safest to divide and ligate biliary branches intrahepatically

## Anatomy: Hepatic Veins

- Three major hepatic veins course through scissurae within intrahepatic sectoral planes:
  - **Right hepatic vein:** right scissura between right anterior and posterior sectors
  - **Middle hepatic vein:** main scissura between right and left hemilivers
  - **Left hepatic vein:** left scissura between segment II posteriorly and segments III/IV anteriorly
- Left and middle hepatic veins commonly join as single common branch before entering vena cava

## Hepatic Veins: Branches and Drainage

- **Right hepatic vein:** branches to right giving major segmental branches to VI and VII
  - Occasionally inferior right hepatic vein(s) present draining segment VI
- **Middle hepatic vein:** principal drainage of anterior sector via dominant branches to VIII and V
  - Typically only small branches to segment IV
- **Left hepatic vein:** segment II branch often enters proximally with extrahepatic course
  - Distal to segment II branch, serves as dominant drainage of segment III

## Anatomy: Umbilical Vein and Vena Cava

- **Umbilical vein:** nearly always present; courses anterior to umbilical fissure between segments III and IV
  - Most commonly drains into left hepatic vein
  - Can drain into middle hepatic vein or confluence of left and middle as trifurcation
- **Vena cava:** borders groove along central strip of posterior liver
  - Right side abuts posterior aspects of segments VI and VII
  - Left side abuts caudate lobe

## Vena Cava: Caval Ligament and Branches

- **Caval ligament:** fibrous tissue with varying hepatic parenchyma wrapping from segment VII around cava to left border of caudate lobe
  - Forms sling around cava
  - Dissecting and dividing essential to expose upper retrohepatic cava and right hepatic vein
- Retrohepatic cava arises just above renal veins
- Small and medium-sized draining branches from posterior liver (mainly caudate) require control and ligation
- Some branches require suture control or stapler division

## Intrahepatic Segmental Branching Patterns

- Hilar vessels invaginated by Glisson capsule forming intrahepatic "pedicles"
- Variation is the rule; preoperative imaging essential
- **Left inflow pedicle:** forms at base of umbilical fissure
  - First branch: cephalad branch to segment II
  - Then: more distal branch to segment III anteriorly
- **Segment IV:** multiple inflow pedicles from transverse portion of left inflow vessels and umbilical fissure

## Right-Sided Intrahepatic Pedicles

- **Main right inflow pedicle:** typically short or nonexistent
  - Branches into anterior and posterior sectoral pedicles
- **Anterior pedicle:** large dominant pedicle cephalad and to the right to segment VIII
  - Gives off multiple small segment V branches
  - Segment VIII branches into ventral and dorsal branches
  - Dorsal branch often arches superiorly over right hepatic vein
- **Posterior pedicle:** often short or nonexistent
  - Segment VI and VII branches commonly arise proximally

## Perihepatic Ligaments and Attachments

- **Ligamentum teres:** runs along abdominal wall, terminates at falciform ligament anterior to liver
  - Carries obliterated umbilical vein and small hepatic artery branch
- Division of falciform ligament cephalad exposes coronary/triangular ligaments covering hepatic veins
- **Right triangular ligament:** broad; divided along plane between right liver and diaphragm
  - Division with rotation of liver to left exposes vena cava and caval ligament
- **Left triangular ligament:** thin; lies just inferior to left phrenic vein

## Figure: Perihepatic Ligaments (Figure 118A.2)

- **Panel A:** Ligamentum teres secured; falciform ligament division begun backward to expose suprahepatic IVC
- **Panel B:** Left triangular ligament exposed and divided with cautery; care taken not to injure left phrenic vein
- **Panel C:** Peritoneal reflection of right triangular ligament incised; mobilization of right liver deepened to display right lateral margin of IVC

## Caudate Lobe Anatomy

- Vascular inflow, biliary drainage, and venous outflow as described previously
- Lies between rest of liver and vena cava except rightmost aspects of right hemiliver
- Anterior sector lies anterior to caudate (does not border cava)
- Right side = **caudate process:** adjacent to posterior border of right inflow pedicles
  - Division critical for exposure of right inflow pedicle(s)
- Left liver lies anterior to caudate (does not abut vena cava except superiorly near hepatic veins)

## Figure: Caudate Lobe Anatomy (Figure 118A.3)

- **Panel A:** Cross-sectional sketch at level of porta hepatis
  - Shows principal caudate branch of left portal vein (LPV)
  - Position of lesser omentum, ligamentum venosum, middle hepatic vein (MHV) separating segments IV and V
  - Posterior ligamentous band joining segments I and VII
- **Panel B:** Caudate lies anterior to IVC but posterior to portal venous structures
  - Blood supply mainly from caudate branch (CV) of LPV
  - Relationships of HA, LHV, LV, RHV, LPV illustrated

## Positioning, Retractors, and Incision

- **Position:** Supine with arms out laterally for peripheral vascular access
- **Table positioning:** Reverse Trendelenburg to drop abdominal viscera and expose liver
- **Rotation:** Right or left-sided rotation used liberally for exposure of different liver parts
- **Retraction:** Cephalad retraction of costal margin at approximately 45-degree angle
  - Lateral retraction of right chest wall and inferior retraction of lower abdominal viscera also helpful

## Figure: Patient Positioning (Figure 118A.4)

- Patient positioned supine on operating table
- Wide exposure of abdomen and chest
- Arms extended laterally
- Cross bar holds large retractor used to elevate costal margin
- Reverse Trendelenburg position facilitates exposure by gravity-assisted caudal displacement of viscera
- Allows surgeon access to both right and left upper quadrants

## Surgical Incisions (Figure 118A.5)

- **A-B-C-D:** Mercedes type incision (bilateral subcostal)
- **D-E:** Median sternotomy extension
- **F:** Right thoracic extension
- **A-B-D:** Extended right subcostal (hockey stick) — most often adequate
- **Midline incision:** useful for combined resections with inferior organs; adequate for left-sided resections
- **Thoracoabdominal extension:** rarely necessary; valuable for caval injury or large right-sided tumors

## General Principles: Four Phases of Major Hepatectomy

- Principal steps broken into four phases:
  1. **Mobilization**
  2. **Inflow control**
  3. **Outflow control**
  4. **Parenchymal transection**
- Order can vary but general principles apply
- Mobilization usually first (except rare anterior approach to right hepatectomy)
- **Critical rule:** Outflow division should NOT be performed before inflow control
  - Results in congested liver parenchyma and venous bleeding

## Inflow Control Strategies

- **Extrahepatic control:** hilar dissection provides early vascular control to liver to be resected
- **Intrahepatic pedicle ligation:** two approaches
  - Divide parenchyma in plane of transection down to pedicles of interest
  - Hepatotomies around inflow pedicle(s) without parenchymal transection
- No demonstrable difference in outcomes between techniques
- Location of tumor may mandate extrahepatic dissection
- Approach at surgeon's discretion unless pathology dictates otherwise

## Outflow Control Strategies

- Can be taken **extrahepatically** as they enter cava or **intrahepatically** after liver division
- **Early extrahepatic venous division:**
  - Additional degree of mobilization
  - Early control of potential bleeding from involved vein
- Pathology or difficulty may make intrahepatic division preferable
- Divide parenchyma back to hepatic vein insertions where they can be taken just as they exit liver

## Parenchymal Transection Principles

- Goal: dissect through parenchyma to expose anticipated anatomy based on preoperative imaging
- Allows appropriate control and division of inflow and outflow structures
- Hepatic transection should be a **dissection**, not frantic hemorrhage control
- Use of coagulating energy devices should not excuse blind coagulation while splitting tissue
- **Intraoperative ultrasound:** critical skill for documenting vascular proximity, patency, flow, and guiding division

## Pringle Maneuver and Hemostasis

- **Pringle maneuver (portal clamping):** not necessary for all cases, but safe and should be prepared for all resections
- Low threshold to transect under Pringle control if bleeding obscures visualization
- **Intermittent clamping preferred** to prevent portal venous congestion
- If dissection has gone well: minimal bleeding beyond minor oozing
- Major bleeding from middle hepatic vein may require suture repair
- First move for venous bleeding: simple compression for a few minutes

## Biliostasis and Drainage

- Meticulous inspection of raw liver surface for bleeding and bile leaks
- Topical hemostatic agents and coagulation devices assist with hemostasis
- Care not to injure contralateral structures with deep sutures or excessive energy
- Routine testing for bile leaks (e.g., air cholangiogram) not proven effective in randomized trials
- Small bile leaks controlled with fine suture repair
- **Drains not recommended** based on randomized trials; leave drain only if ongoing bile leakage

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Mobilization

- Divide ligamentum teres and falciform ligament
- Divide right coronary and triangular ligaments back to hepatic veins
- **Right phrenic vein:** easily visualized landmark draining to cava near right hepatic vein
- Dissect groove between right and middle hepatic vein to origin
- Turn liver to left and inferiorly; divide broad right triangular ligament to expose bare area
- Divide inferior border of right triangular ligament from cava around toward prior dissection

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Caval and Adrenal Dissection

- Retract liver off vena cava to the left
- Dissect right adrenal gland off liver and drop back into retroperitoneum
- Adrenal sometimes adherent; may require deliberate dissection or leave attached with hemostasis
- Dissect superior border of caval ligament and lateral aspect of cava/right hepatic vein
- Dissect anterior border of cava from inferior to superior, controlling retrohepatic caval branches
- Take inferior right hepatic veins at this time

## Figure: Caval Ligament Division (Figure 118A.1)

- **Panel A:** Caval ligament mobilized; clamp passed beneath it; divided with Endo GIA vascular stapler
- **Panel B:** Retrohepatic IVC fully exposed after division
- Dissecting, controlling, and dividing this ligament essential to:
  - Expose upper retrohepatic cava
  - Expose right hepatic vein laterally
  - Mobilize caudate lobe
- Typically more caval branches encountered between ligament and base of right hepatic vein

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Hepatic Vein Control

- Space between caval ligament and lateral border of cava/right hepatic vein dissected with curved blunt clamp
- Once encircled and cava/right hepatic vein protected, divide caval ligament (vascular load stapler convenient)
- Dissect, control, and divide caval branches up until base of right hepatic vein exposed
- **Tunnel between right and middle hepatic vein:**
  - Wide avascular plane
  - Dissected from above and below
  - Plane curves anteriorly when approached from below
- Encircle right hepatic vein for later division

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Inflow Control (Extrahepatic)

- Lower hilar plate with incision in peritoneal reflection at base of segment IV
- Perform cholecystectomy; retract cystic duct stump to left
- Exposes right hepatic artery in groove between bile duct and portal vein
- If right hepatic artery anterior (known from imaging), dissect anterior to bile duct
- Encircle right hepatic artery; clamp and confirm pulse at base of umbilical fissure in left hepatic artery
- Divide right hepatic artery; retract proximal artery to left as sling

## Figure: Extrahepatic Vascular Control (Figure 118A.6)

- **Panel A:** Right hepatic duct dissected; confluence of hepatic ducts and origin of left hepatic duct shown
- **Panel B:** Right hepatic duct divided; traction on cystic duct and right hepatic duct stump exposes vessels beneath; right hepatic artery dissected and divided
- **Panel C:** Right portal vein dissected; forceps passed beneath it; caudate branch sought and ligated; vascular clamps applied
- **Panel D:** Vein divided; proximal stump oversewn with vascular suture; distal stump ligated
- **Panel E:** Photograph showing main PV giving rise to anterior and posterior sectoral branches independently

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Portal Vein and Bile Duct

- Dissect portal vein exposing main, right, and left portal veins
- Retract biliary tree anteriorly and to the right; vein retractor helpful
- Critical to see anatomy of both right and left portal veins
- Identify and ligate branch to caudate process (nearly always present)
- Encircle right portal vein with clear visualization of main and left portal vein
- Clamp and note demarcation; document portal flow to left liver with Doppler ultrasound
- Divide right bile duct inside liver within pedicles to maximize distance from left bile duct

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Pedicle Ligation Approach

- **Anterior approach:** Split liver parenchyma in principal plane toward inflow; encircle main right pedicle or sectoral pedicles at origin
- **Hepatotomy approach:** Flanking incisions in caudate process and base of gallbladder fossa; encircle pedicles with finger or blunt-angled clamp
- Middle hepatic vein and segment V branches drape over right inflow pedicle — must be anticipated
- Ensure flow to left liver before division of pedicles
- Anterior approach without mobilization described for large right-sided hepatocellular carcinoma

## Figure: Intrahepatic Pedicle Control (Figure 118A.7)

- **Panel A:** Intrahepatic control of portal pedicles (1), parenchymal transection (2), subsequent intrahepatic control of hepatic veins (3)
- **Panel B:** Approach to right portal pedicle after liver mobilized from IVC; hepatotomies in gallbladder fossa and caudate process indicated by curved arrows
- **Panel C:** Digital isolation of right pedicle
- **Panel D:** Photograph showing finger insertion through hepatotomy in caudate lobe merging with gallbladder fossa to isolate right portal pedicle

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Parenchymal Transection

- Middle hepatic vein is plane between right and left liver
- Decide which side of middle hepatic vein dissection will proceed
- Preferable to **preserve middle hepatic vein** by dissecting along its right side
- Identify middle hepatic vein and take branches to segment V (draped over anterior sectoral pedicle)
- Expose right inflow pedicles; incise caudate process and encircle/divide pedicle(s)
- Ensure distance from left inflow and bile duct; ensure left liver flow throughout

## Right Hemihepatectomy: Completing Transection

- Transection commences along middle hepatic vein toward cava
- Branches to segment VIII carefully anticipated, dissected, encircled, and divided
- Most common hemorrhage sources: injuries to segment VIII branches or middle hepatic vein itself
- Continue to base of right hepatic vein and through posterior aspect to complete resection
- If right hepatic vein not taken before transection, approach at end intrahepatically or at origin
- Right hepatectomy can be performed to left of middle hepatic vein preserving segment IV

## Extended Right Hepatectomy and Right Trisectionectomy

- Follows steps for right hepatectomy as detailed previously
- **Extended right hepatectomy:** encompasses part of segment IV; removes at least some of middle hepatic vein
- **Right trisectionectomy:** removes all of segment IV and middle hepatic vein at its origin
- Additional inflow steps: taking segment IV inflow vessels most easily within parenchyma during transection to right of umbilical fissure
- If mandated by pathology, dissection within umbilical fissure — ensure protection of segments II/III inflow/biliary branches

## Figure: Pedicle Distribution at Base of Left Liver (Figure 118A.8)

- **A:** Pedicle to left liver including segment I
- **B:** Pedicle to left liver, sparing segment I
- **C:** Pedicle to segment II
- **D:** Pedicle to segment III
- **E1:** Pedicle to segment IVb
- **E2:** Pedicle to segment IVa
- Illustrates points of division for various extents of left-sided resection
- Critical reference for extended right and left resections involving segment IV

## Figure: Segment IV Inflow Control (Figure 118A.9)

- Feedback vessels from left portal triad secured in parenchyma just slightly to right of falciform ligament
- If tumor adjacent to segment IV, dissection must be within umbilical fissure
- More safely carried out within liver tissue just to right of falciform ligament
- Preliminary suture ligation within umbilical fissure illustrated
- Procedure deprives segment IV of its blood supply

## Extended Right Hepatectomy: Outflow and Transection

- How and where middle hepatic vein divided should be planned preoperatively
- Most effective division from within liver (origin located intrahepatically where it joins left hepatic vein)
- For extended resection: decide level of middle hepatic vein transection with attention to branches to V and VIII
- For formal trisectionectomy: middle hepatic vein typically taken at or near origin
- Identify origin during transection with careful attention to protect left hepatic vein and common channel

## Extended Right Hepatectomy: Vein Preservation Considerations

- Once right hepatic vein divided, right border of middle hepatic vein more easily visualized, dissected, encircled
- Rarely needed; best to have good exposure of suprahepatic cava before this maneuver
- **Umbilical vein** (drains into left hepatic vein commonly) should be identified and preserved
- If umbilical vein drains into middle hepatic vein, must address specifically to preserve left hepatic vein
- **Injury to left hepatic vein:** severe life-threatening injury disrupting nearly all venous outflow from remnant

## Extended Right Hepatectomy: Parenchymal Details

- Transection requires identification of segment IV inflow and middle hepatic vein
- Key issue: transection requires sharp right turn at base of segment IV
- Does not continue as straight line (would proceed directly into left inflow)
- Awkward dissection but critical to protect left-sided inflow/biliary structures
- If preserving middle hepatic vein, clamp at planned transection point and observe venous flow from left liver before division

## Left Hepatectomy: Mobilization

- More straightforward than right liver mobilization
- Left liver lies anterior to caudate; does not abut vena cava except superior-most border
- Divide ligamentum teres and falciform ligament back to hepatic veins
- Identify groove between middle and right hepatic vein (marks superior border between right and left liver)
- Dissect and expose common channel between middle and left hepatic vein; define lateral border

## Figure: Left and Middle Hepatic Veins (Figure 118A.10)

- **Panel A:** Left lateral section completely mobilized from diaphragm and turned to right; gastrohepatic ligament divided; line of ligamentum venosum exposed
- **Panel B:** Ligamentum venosum divided exposing window between vena cava and left hepatic vein
- Dissection in this space allows dissection of left and middle hepatic veins separately or together
- Veins clamped, divided, and oversewn or divided with Endo GIA vascular stapler
- Applicable to left hepatectomy and extended left hepatectomy

## Left Hepatectomy: Hepatic Vein and Inflow Control

- Divide left triangular ligament from lateral to medial up to lateral border of left hepatic vein/common channel
- Care to identify and avoid left phrenic vein
- Retract left lateral section to right; divide lesser omentum and ligamentum venosum just before entry into left hepatic vein
- Expose narrow plane inferior to hepatic veins and superior to caudate
- Incise peritoneal attachments along superior border of caudate to expose space
- Preferable to control left and middle hepatic veins at origins extrahepatically

## Left Hepatectomy: Inflow Control (Extrahepatic)

- Extrahepatic control preferable because more easily accessible than on right
- Cholecystectomy; note anatomy of common bile and hepatic duct
- Dissect left side of porta hepatis; most anterior structure is left hepatic artery
- Dissect along left border of porta hepatis and encircle
- Dissect branching of right and left hepatic artery to confirm anatomy and protect right hepatic artery
- Deliberate dissection of proximal right hepatic artery identifies segment IV branches from right (common finding)

## Figure: Left Hepatectomy Dissection (Figure 118A.11)

- **Panel A:** Dissection for left hepatectomy at base of umbilical fissure
- **Panel B:** Left hepatic duct (LHD) divided at base of umbilical fissure
- **A1:** Point of division of left hepatic artery for concomitant removal of caudate lobe
- **A2:** Point of division of left hepatic artery for left hepatectomy
- **P1:** Point of division of left portal vein for left hepatectomy and caudate resection
- **P2:** Point of division of left portal vein for left hepatectomy

## Left Hepatectomy: Arterial and Portal Control

- Identify replaced or accessory left hepatic arteries within lesser omentum toward base of umbilical fissure
- Test clamp left arterial inflow; ensure pulse remains on right side of porta hepatis
- Ligate and divide arteries, exposing underlying main and left portal vein
- Retract biliary tree and left hepatic artery stumps; dissect right, left, and main portal veins
- Identify caudate branch off left portal vein and protect it
- Encircle left portal vein between caudate branch and ligamentum venosum insertion

## Left Hepatectomy: Biliary and Venous Division

- Small portal branches to segment IV should be sought and controlled
- Clamp left portal vein; document demarcation and right portal flow grossly and by Doppler ultrasound
- Due to common variation of right sectoral ducts draining into left bile duct, best practice to divide left bile duct in left main pedicle
- If tumor mandates division in porta hepatis, dissect duct and any branches carefully
- Protection of right bile duct and aberrant right sectoral branches critical
- Low threshold for cholangiography if any concern

## Left Hepatectomy: Parenchymal Transection

- Commence transection; determine if to left or right of middle hepatic vein
- Note origin of umbilical vein (based on imaging and ultrasound) to avoid injury
- Transection through principal plane starts from anterior surface toward plane of ligamentum venosum, preserving underlying caudate
- If to left of middle hepatic vein: no typically dominant branches, though umbilical vein may originate from middle hepatic vein proximally
- If to right of middle hepatic vein: anticipate and control segment V and VIII venous branches

## Extended Left Hepatectomy

- Includes left liver along with incomplete portion of segment V and/or VIII
- Parenchymal transection to right of middle hepatic vein for at least some of its course
- Mobilization and inflow/outflow control same as left hepatectomy
- Preferable to have extrahepatic control of left and middle hepatic veins before transection
- If not feasible, split liver back to space between middle and right hepatic vein and take veins after transection

## Figure: Extended Left Hepatectomy (Figure 118A.12)

- Liver tissue entered for parenchymal transection just anterior to estimated lower limit of right scissura
- Plane followed toward base of gallbladder fossa and point of entry of right hepatic duct into liver substance
- Anterior sectional vessels and bile ducts identified in liver substance (arrow) and can be controlled
- Illustrates the anterior approach to the right anterior sectoral pedicle during extended left resection

## Extended Left Hepatectomy: Anterior Sector Management

- Specific extent of anterior sector to be resected must be planned and dissected specifically
- Some or all of segment V or VIII can be taken depending on individualized anatomy
- Inflow anatomy to these segments critical to plan
- Ill-advised extension into anterior sectoral pedicles without appropriate parenchymal resection can leave ischemic liver behind
- Inflow vessels to resected anterior sector taken intrahepatically during transection

## Left Trisectionectomy

- Challenging operation removing left liver en bloc with segment V and VIII of right liver
- By definition: left and middle hepatic veins taken at their origin
- Complete mobilization of liver advisable using techniques for right and left liver
- Three hepatic veins dissected at origin; preferable to encircle left and middle hepatic veins at insertion into vena cava
- Right hepatic vein insertion should be visible; critical element is preservation of right hepatic vein

## Figure: Left Trisectionectomy Result (Figure 118A.13)

- Liver substance removed anterior to posterior sectional ducts and vessels
- Upper part of parenchymal dissection runs just anterior to right hepatic vein
- Involves control of middle and left hepatic veins
- After resection, right posterior sectional portal triad visible branching on surface of exposed liver
- Demonstrates the extent of resection and preservation of posterior sector

## Left Trisectionectomy: Inflow Control

- Inflow and outflow control for left liver as described earlier
- Two options for right anterior sectoral inflow:
  - **Preferred:** Take anterior sectoral inflow as pedicle inside liver via hepatotomies or after splitting liver in right scissura to base of pedicle
  - **Alternative:** Dissection in porta hepatis to identify anterior sectoral portal and arterial branches (tedious, risks injury to posterior sectoral vessels)
- Taking inflow early shows demarcation but not necessary
- Assess flow grossly and by Doppler to ensure posterior sector perfusion

## Left Trisectionectomy: Transection and Outflow

- Transection marked by plane of right hepatic vein (identified by ultrasound)
- Regardless of inflow technique, critical to assess flow grossly and by Doppler to ensure posterior sector perfusion
- If anterior sectoral inflow taken in porta, still advisable to take anterior sectoral bile duct within liver for distance from posterior sector
- Transection plane to left of right hepatic vein ultimately heading toward ligamentum venosum
- Usually no dominant leftward branches off right hepatic vein

## Left Trisectionectomy: Critical Details

- Dorsal inflow branch to segment VIII feeds parenchyma superior and to right of right hepatic vein
- Must be anticipated and resected to avoid leaving ischemic liver behind
- Transection curves to left, anterior to intrahepatic caudate, toward base of anterior sectoral pedicle
- Once anterior sectoral pedicle divided and left inflow taken, left and middle hepatic veins taken at origin
- Alternatively, veins taken at end of transection
- After anterior pedicle division, transection curves to left to base of segment IV; left biliary tree taken with left liver pedicle at base of umbilical fissure

## En Bloc Caudate Resection: Indications and Principles

- Clinical scenarios: hilar cholangiocarcinoma, large tumors extending into caudate
- Understanding typical and individual anatomy critical
- Critical element: complete mobilization of caudate from cava
- For right-sided resections: caval dissection continues to left dissecting caudate off cava
- Caval ligament at left side of caudate must be divided after mobilizing and retracting left lateral section

## Figure: Caudate Mobilization (Figure 118A.14)

- Lesser omentum opened; caudate branch of left portal vein tied
- Ligamentous attachments of caudate posteriorly opened
- Dissection of retrohepatic caudate veins approached from right or left side
- Arrows indicate lines of approach to free caudate lobe
- IVC, MHV, and LPV relationships shown

## Figure: Caudate Parenchymal Dissection (Figure 118A.15)

- Parenchymal phase of dissection shown with arrows
- Proximity of left hepatic vein (LHV) and middle hepatic vein (MHV)
- Right portion of caudate lobe lies just to left of MHV
- Retrohepatic caudate veins controlled with clips
- Demonstrates the intimate relationship between caudate and major hepatic veins

## Caudate Resection: Technical Execution

- Retrohepatic caval branches serially dissected and divided between clips or ties
- Commonly a large branch centrally requiring suture control or stapler division
- Inflow and biliary drainage originate proximally from both right and left main branches
- For right-sided resections: inflow to left side of caudate taken at base of umbilical fissure (branches from left portal vein and hepatic artery)
- Small biliary branches encountered and controlled with ties or clips

## Caudate Resection: Right and Left Approaches

- **Right-sided:** After left caudate inflow taken, mobilize caudate to place on right side of vena cava; branch to caudate process taken with right portal vein; right hepatectomy performed as described; caudate retracted to right and included as transection proceeds to left of caudate process; ensure caudate completely free of cava and left-sided structures
- **Left-sided:** More intuitive; majority of caudate is left-sided structure; caudate process can be preserved; mobilize as described; origins of left and middle hepatic veins more easily exposed; inflow to left caudate taken proximally ensuring inclusion

## Caudate Resection: Biliary Considerations

- Left-sided resection with caudate mandates biliary dissection in extrahepatic location
- Biliary anatomy must be elucidated; left duct taken proximally in porta hepatis
- Duct taken sharply and probed to confirm anatomy and patency of main and right bile ducts
- Low threshold to perform cholangiogram if any concern
- Right sectoral ducts draining into left bile duct should be identified and preserved if possible; otherwise reconstruction may be needed

## Summary: Key Principles

- Major hepatic resections: technically difficult and morbid
- Require extensive mobilization and expertise in working anatomy
- Vascular control and preservation of contralateral structures are critical
- Failure can result in hemorrhage, ischemia of remnant, liver failure, or death
- Anatomic variation common; each case must be individualized
- Technique must be appropriately adapted to specific anatomy and pathology

## Summary: Clinical Approach

- Operations of last resort; only performed when mandated by underlying pathology
- Large tumors and central tumors involving vasculature are typical indications
- Parenchymal-sparing resections much preferred whenever possible
- Risk of major morbidity and liver failure significantly lower with parenchymal-sparing approaches
- Extensive training and experience critical for:
  - Judgment regarding when to use major hepatic resection
  - Technical skill to successfully navigate these operations
